items.body:
Breezy new age house by an Antipodean artist with illustrious credits beside Michal Hutchence, Bono, Jamiroquai since the ‘80s, evened out with Kuniyuki and 451 remixes...

"Originally emerging from Melbourne’s post-punk and new wave underground in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Gus Till has spent more than four decades navigating a remarkably diverse musical path. From early electronic experimentation with Third Eye alongside Ollie Olsen, through a pivotal role in the formative years of the global psy-trance movement and collaborations with artists including Michael Hutchence, System 7, Manu Dibango, Todd Terry and Bim Sherman, Till’s work has consistently resisted easy categorisation, moving fluidly between ambient music, downtempo, house, trance and psychedelic electronica.

First released on Japan’s Dakini Records in 2006, ‘Rainsong’ captures many of these threads in a single expansive composition. Built around a pulsating bassline, layered live percussion and soaring vocal elements, the track sits comfortably between the dancefloor and more immersive listening environments. Unfolding patiently across nearly thirteen minutes, it combines hypnotic rhythmic momentum with a rich sense of atmosphere and musicality.

For the B-side, Kuniyuki Takahashi offers a distinct reinterpretation of the original. His remix gradually unfolds from a patient introduction into a deep and richly textured exploration of the track’s core themes. Subtle spatial processing, nuanced arrangement shifts and his unmistakable sense of atmosphere transform the source material while preserving its emotional core."

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

items.body: Some musicians seem destined to play together at some point. Not always at the beginning of their careers, but as their music develops, it feels as if their paths are compelled to cross. Gustafsson and Pohjonen have been in the other’s orbit for some time, but it took a suggestion from Bogdan Benigar that the duo perform together at the 2024 Ljubljana Music Festival to provide the impetus and foundation of a pairing that has since enlivened stages at events such as the Tampere Jazz Happening in 2024, where their energised performance impressed audiences. Finnish accordionist Kimmo Pohjonen plays the accordion in ways you would not imagine. He creates music that changes how the instrument is viewed. With roots in regional folk and classical music, Pohjonen is also influenced by rock and punk. He has written string music for the acclaimed Kronos Quartet and played in the art-rock band KTU alongside King Crimson percussionist Pat Mastelotto and Trey Gunn. Pohjonen uses accordions with additions to create enhanced effects, and his delivery has revolutionised accordion music and visual performances. He has, in effect, created a genre of his own, with the accordion at its heart. For the last thirty years, he has toured the world, taking part in events, festivals, and playing in different venues. His solo 5-row accordion project featured extreme and original compositions with effects and performances with lights and sounds. His custom-made accordion, along with his imaginative playing, has given him a renown as one of music’s most intriguing characters. He has released several albums and toured extensively in Europe, Asia, and America. Swedish musician Mats Gustafsson needs little introduction to improvised music appreciators and is also known for his experimental music, his diversions into punk, rock, classical, and his dynamic performances. He has composed for orchestras, created solo recordings, and toured extensively, as well as being a writer for jazz magazines. Both musicians have strong stage presence and dynamic personalities, yet each is capable of pulling back to leave space. Their strong personalities could see them clash, but they also have the altruism and connection to others that true musicians possess, so as a duo, they create music both individual to each musician and that stands as duo work. Their similarities and differences combine to create a connection where they are pushed to excel beyond their normal range. It is clear from this recording that ‘Two Balls Are Enough’ brings together kindred spirits, each of whom contributes equally. Gustafsson told me, “The duo was initiated by Bogdan Benigar, a mutual friend of Pohjonen and me. I have admired Kimmo for years. He may be slightly from another side of the improvised music spectrum, but the energy he is playing with is very appealing. He has amazing levels of energy, and the vibe and feel of the music is one hundred percent 100 % DIY. We are both the same age, and both spring from punk rock in our teens. Our stupid interest in ice hockey and saunas unites us even more. This is just the beginning. The way Kimmo is using samplers and electronics with his accordion is heaven-sent.” Both appreciate the capabilities of their instruments but embrace technology and effects that enhance and work with the sonic measurements of their instruments. Since that inspired curation in 2024, they have been blending their sound worlds, and ‘Two Balls are Enough’ is their first album out on Trost Records. The opener, ‘Ice Heaven’ is a fierce, sparking, energy-laden piece, with intricate, heavy rhythmic patterns, backed by harmonics between the two musicians that bind and create a wholeness to the divergent patterns. Gustafsson unleashes a stentorian solo, while Pohjonen maintains harmonies and high-energy, powerful lines behind. The unified lines are loud, forceful, and incredibly effective in contrast. ‘Magna’ combines chords from the accordion with electronics and screaming effects across a pounding, intense litany of rhythms. A piece of three sections, divided by total silences, this is an intriguing listen. And wholly irreverent. ‘Snow.Linat’ is gentle, with Gustafsson’s flute floating, whispering over the constantly shifting soundscape foundation. Some sections feel powerful and intense, with the flute slashing through, contrasting with emotive, delicate sections, where the accordion’s voice sings, adorned with breathy vocal tones. The sudden shift to a powerful, pithy solo from the sax is gorgeous, and the intensity becomes palpable. The title track is a messy, joyful, eclectic mix of pops, whistles, accordion chords, and electronic effects, into which Gustafsson’s flute weaves and dives. The track sums up the essence of the album, distilled into just over two minutes of chaotic mayhem, while ‘Its Body Falls Open’ is a tinkling, high-pitched maelstrom of swirling sounds and effects, topped by Gustafsson’s eccentric sax playing and jittering accordion, with ‘Worn Out Words’ providing more of the same. ‘Slow Down The Beating’ is a track that creates deep impact. It has gentleness, with the flute introducing a melodic section before a percussive deluge of changing patterns. This is backed by intricate beats and rhythms, and a development into a raw, pared-back piece with some beautiful rhythmic clashes and dynamic changes over a steady background beat. ‘Naga’ is an exemplar of interaction between two minds with chaotic intent, yet a definitive directive, the result of which is a confident exchange of ideas, manifestations and rhythms that rise and fall, creating an engaging listen. The musical foundations shape-shift, creating powerful imagery and an aural dynamism that evokes spirit. The tautness of the atmosphere is tempered with melodic lines from Gustafsson, as well as his fulgurating, strident phrasing. “Backengrillen 1” (maybe named after the punk band Gustafsson plays in) creates epic grandeur yet is surprisingly intimate and filled with rustic beauty. The repeated melody on the sax intensifies and provides a gentler interlude before Gustafsson varies the phrasing, and all the while the rapid accordion runs provide a tight but moving backdrop. Gustafsson and Pohjonen have been touring regularly over the last couple of years, and the release of ‘Two Balls are Enough’ demonstrates the powerful connection these two musicians have. I commented to Gustafsson that the accordion was not an instrument I really liked – until I heard this. His response was, “Same here - it was never my favourite instrument, but after working with Kimmo, and also some insane Norwegian players: Kalle Moberg, and Ida Lövli (fantastic!) and Frode Hatli - I had to change my mind. It is a funny instrument!. I never thought I would work seriously with anyone playing it, but ha!” (Moberg has recorded with Nilssen Love, Hakion thelin and many more, Lovli recorded her debut album Skumring (Twilight) on Lawo Classics, and Hatli is a composer who has released several albums and is part of multicultural projects worldwide). Recordings like this unite different genres and also expand the possibilities of instruments, and maybe, just maybe, change how we hear and feel music. To quote Gustafsson – “This is just the beginning.” Two Balls Are Enough by Mats Gustafsson / Kimmo Pohjonen Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
For no na, returning to Head In The Clouds feels a little like coming home. The popular Indonesian girl group sees the 88rising festival in Los Angeles as more than another stop on the calendar — it is a reunion with fellow artists, collaborators, and the community that has followed their journey so far.

This year’s performance also marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter. Fresh from announcing their debut album, island girl, due out on 18 September via 88rising, the quartet are preparing to bring their confident, playful energy — and plenty of Indonesian pride — to the festival stage.

Ahead of their appearance, no na spoke to Bandwagon about their dream surprise guest, the performance moments fans should watch out for, and what it means to put +62 on the global pop map.

Head In The Clouds brings together artists from across Asia and the diaspora in one place. Looking at this year’s lineup, who are you most excited to catch live, and why?

Honestly, HITC’s lineup always feels like a family reunion for us, since we met up at last year’s festival as well. We’re excited to reconnect with Brian — he actually sang background vocals on our new single, 'honk!'

If Head In The Clouds had a “dream surprise stage”, who would you want to see walk out?

If HITC had a dream surprise stage, we would love to see Silk Sonic!

Every festival has its own personality. If you had to describe the vibe you’re hoping to create at Head In The Clouds in just three words, what would they be?

Confident, playful, island girl — can we count that as one word? (Laughs)

Festivals often bring in fans who may be seeing you live for the very first time. What is one song or moment in your set that you hope they will walk away remembering?

Probably a tie between performing our new song, 'honk!', and the choreography for our dance break. It’s our first performance since announcing our debut album, island girl, which is out on 18 September via 88rising, so we’re excited to celebrate with everyone.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Head In The Clouds Festival (@hitcfestival)

As an Indonesian group performing at Head In The Clouds, what does it mean to share a piece of Southeast Asia with a global audience?

Everything, honestly. We grew up wanting the world to see Indonesia as more than just a beautiful backdrop — we want people to hear it, feel our rhythms, see our dances, and have our culture woven into pop music that can stand next to anything else on that lineup. Every stage we get is one more chance to put +62 on the map, on our own terms.

items.body:
BTS returned to the North American stage with two sold-out nights at MetLife Stadium, bringing 157,000 fans into the expansive world of ARIRANG.

Held on 1 and 2 August, the concerts marked the opening of the second North American leg of BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’. The shows arrived days after the group headlined the first FIFA World Cup Final Halftime Show and followed a sold-out European stadium run that drew more than 717,000 concertgoers.

At MetLife Stadium, BTS performed on a 360-degree stage built around the tour’s visual universe. Korean artistic traditions met the scale and spectacle of a contemporary stadium production, reflecting ARIRANG’s themes across one of North America’s biggest concert venues.

The setlist featured tracks from the group’s fifth studio album, ARIRANG, including ‘SWIM’, ‘2.0’, ‘Hooligan’, and ‘Like Animals’. Career-spanning favourites ‘Butter’ and ‘Dynamite’ also made their way into the show, giving the packed stadium plenty of familiar moments to sing and move along to.

The performances extended beyond New Jersey through BTS THE CITY ARIRANG NEW YORK, a citywide project that transformed locations across New York into interactive spaces for ARMY.

The Korean Cultural Center New York and Grand Central Terminal hosted ARMY "MADANG" gathering points, where fans could customise light sticks and T-shirts. Visitors could also view stage outfits from BTS’ historic LOVE YOURSELF: SPEAK YOURSELF concerts at Wembley Stadium.

Elsewhere, a Random Play Dance took over Times Square, while Top of the Rock and Arte Museum New York brought elements of the ARIRANG visual world into the city. A Stamp Rally connected participating cultural venues and partner locations across Manhattan. As part of the programme, Bank of Hope pledged US$1 for every Stamp Rally check-in at its Manhattan branch to support financial literacy education through its Hope Delivered initiative.

With the MetLife Stadium dates completed, BTS will take the tour to Foxborough, Baltimore, Dallas, Toronto, Chicago, and Los Angeles.

items.body:
Over October are preparing for the biggest headline show of their career at the New Frontier Theater, taking place on 4 October in Quezon City.

The concert arrives after two sold-out performances at the Music Museum and the band's successful anniversary show at MOA Sky, marking another milestone as the Filipino alternative pop outfit celebrates 12 years together. More significantly, the show will serve as drummer Janessa "Janae" Geronimo's farewell performance, making it the final official concert featuring the band's original five-member lineup before they enter a new chapter.

Speaking about the upcoming transition, the band shared that Janessa's departure has brought a mix of emotions: "For better or for worse, Janessa's departure is something we will all have to come to terms with. We're all, for the most part, excited for both Over October's and Janessa's respective new chapters. But of course, we also feel that a good thing is about to come to an end."

The band also acknowledged that moving forward without one of its founding members remains an adjustment, but emphasised that their friendship extends beyond the stage. While the creative process may evolve, their immediate focus remains on delivering their strongest performances in the months leading up to the concert.

Over the past 12 years, Over October have become one of the Philippines' defining alternative pop acts, building a devoted fanbase through heartfelt songwriting, memorable live shows, and songs that have resonated with a generation of listeners. Looking back on their journey, the band said that the memories they've created together are just as meaningful as their streaming achievements and sold-out concerts.

Rather than simply celebrating milestones, Over October Live at the New Frontier Theater promises to reflect on the band's story so far while giving fans one final opportunity to witness the original lineup share the stage together.

items.body:
aespa are keeping the momentum going following their landmark 2 August Lollapalooza debut in Chicago with the release of the music video for 'Switchblade', their collaboration with Ty Dolla $ign.

The visual arrives just days after the K-pop quartet took over the Allianz Stage at Grant Park, where fans were treated to one of the festival's biggest surprises. During a performance of 'Switchblade', Ty Dolla $ign emerged onstage, marking the first time the collaborators had performed the track live together.

Backed by a live band, DJ, and dancers, KARINA, GISELLE, WINTER, and NINGNING delivered a 14-song set that balanced career-defining hits with the live debut of several tracks from their second studio album, LEMONADE. Opening with 'Black Mamba', the group powered through fan favourites including 'Next Level', 'Armageddon', 'Supernova', and 'Whiplash' before introducing new material from the record.

Credit: Andrea Escobar-Garcia for Lollapalooza

Alongside its double title tracks 'WDA' and 'LEMONADE', the group also performed fan-favourite B-sides 'Can't Help Myself', 'Switchblade (Feat. Ty Dolla $ign)', and 'SHAKIN'' live for the first time. The set was streamed globally via Hulu in the United States, Disney+ in international markets, and Weverse in select regions including South Korea.

Reflecting on the surprise collaboration, Ty Dolla $ign shared: "It was an incredible experience to be back on stage at Lollapalooza—this time alongside aespa. So proud of how far they've come. Watching their journey and seeing them own a stage like this is truly inspiring. Congratulations on another unforgettable show!"

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Pop Base (@popbase)

The group closed the performance with 'LEMONADE', bringing its first appearance at the iconic festival to an electrifying finish.

Speaking after the show, aespa said: "This was our first time performing at Lollapalooza, and it was such an honor to take the stage in Chicago. Hearing the crowd sing along and cheer throughout the set gave us so much energy, and we had an incredible time performing. We're so grateful to everyone who came out to support us. We hope to carry all of that energy with us as we head into our upcoming world tour."

Credit: Andrea Escobar-Garcia for Lollapalooza

Following Lollapalooza, aespa will kick off its fourth world tour, 2026-27 aespa LIVE TOUR - SYNK : COMPLæXITY, with two shows in Seoul on 7 and 8 August. The tour will continue across Asia, Latin America, North America, the U.K. and Europe. Tickets are on sale now at aespaworldtour.com.

items.body:
Rainbow Disco Club Singapore has unveiled the full lineup for its highly anticipated debut edition, with acclaimed selectors and live acts from Japan, Hong Kong, and Singapore set to take over the city on 3–4 October.

Leading the bill are Antal, founder of the influential Rush Hour Records and one of dance music's most respected crate-diggers; Japanese electronic music pioneer Kuniyuki; revered techno figure DJ Nobu; and Hong Kong-based DJ and producer Xiaolin. The festival is co-organised with Singapore party collective Ice Cream Sundays and will unfold across three sessions.

The open-air Day Session, taking place at Block 39 Carpark in Tanjong Pagar Distripark from 1 PM to 10:15 PM on 3 October, will feature a live performance from Kuniyuki alongside Antal's DJ set. They will be joined by Daryl Knows of Singapore's Darker Than Wax and Tokyo-based Ice Cream Sundays resident Muto.

Inspired by Rainbow Disco Club's flagship festival in Izu, Japan, the daytime programme aims to recreate its laid-back, community-focused atmosphere, where music lovers and families gather in the same space. Alongside the performances, attendees can look forward to casual all-ages activities, games, and a curated selection of food vendors throughout the day.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Rainbow Disco Club (@rainbowdiscoclub)

As night falls, the festival heads indoors for the Night Session at Cargo39, where DJ Nobu and Xiaolin will guide dancers through deep, hypnotic, late-night sounds from 10 PM until 3 AM.

The weekend concludes on 4 October with the Recovery Session at RASA, featuring a rare collaborative live performance from Kin Leonn, Kuniyuki, and Xiaolin, who will perform together as a trio for the first time. Singapore selector Kindergarchy will also soundtrack the closing session with a DJ set of ambient textures and melodic soundscapes.

Following last month's well-received blind sale, Category 1 tickets are now available. Festival-goers can choose from All Sessions passes, Day + Night passes, or individual session tickets. Children aged 12 and below can attend the Day Session without a ticket. Purchase tickets here.

items.body:
Singaporean DJ, producer, and erhu player LIKKI has reached a new career high, making her debut at Tomorrowland Belgium on 25 July.

The artist, whose real name is Likie Low, performed at the House of Fortune by JBL stage during the festival’s second weekend in Boom, Belgium. She joined an international lineup that included Mosimann, Carly Wilford, Rassix, Gaddi, TOO BIASED, and Triciaa.

LIKKI’s appearance followed her participation in the JBL Music Academy’s 2025 cohort. Eight artists from the programme were selected to perform at Tomorrowland, with JBL describing the Singapore-based musician’s work as a series of “cinematic, genre-bending journeys”.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by LIKKI (@theycallmelikki)

Long before stepping behind the decks at one of electronic music’s most prominent festivals, LIKKI built her musical foundation through the erhu and Chinese orchestral music.

The former Singapore National Youth Chinese Orchestra member studied composition at the Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music, where her projects brought electronic dance music together with brass, strings, vocals, and erhu. She has since developed a performance style that moves between future house, trance, and techno while keeping traditional Chinese instruments and orchestral arrangements at its centre.

Rather than using the erhu as a brief embellishment, LIKKI has made the instrument an essential part of her artistic identity. Her live productions have placed DJ sets alongside Chinese instruments, brass ensembles, and concert-hall arrangements—building a bridge between the musical traditions she grew up with and the dance music she discovered as a teenager.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by LIKKI (@theycallmelikki)

Her Tomorrowland debut places her among a small number of Singaporean artists documented to have performed at the Belgian festival.

MYRNE became the first Singaporean act to take the Tomorrowland stage in 2018. DJ-producer Toska followed in 2024. LIKKI now joins them in bringing Singapore’s electronic music scene to the global festival.

Beyond being a personal milestone, the appearance offered LIKKI an international platform for an electronic sound shaped visibly by her Singaporean and Chinese musical roots. Her journey from youth orchestra rehearsals to Tomorrowland demonstrates that tradition does not have to be left outside the club—it can be part of what drives the dance floor forward.

items.body: Simi Fyda‘s In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn offers no gentle introduction. Compared to Yuri (2023), it works within a noticeably narrower palette. The bright contrasts of its predecessor have given way to a largely monochrome world, built from minute variations of timbre, pressure and pitch. Many of the preoccupations of Yuri remain, but they are pursued with greater concentration. The music repeatedly folds back on itself, testing how much tension can be extracted from the smallest amount of material. The opening track, “-may-care”, signals a state of abrasion, establishing an atmosphere of metallic coldness that hangs over the entire record. “maso chords” introduces a faint current of nostalgia, its harmonies carrying the suggestion of something remembered yet irretrievable. From there, the material grows steadily more compressed. “idle hands” simmers without release, while “hedo chords” circles obsessively around recurring intervals and frozen harmonic figures. By the time “mono chords” arrives, repetition itself has become the subject. Minute tonal inflections slowly reshape the surface until the music seems to trap itself inside its own logic, producing a sense of claustrophobia without ever resorting to excess. Originally conceived as an octophonic installation before being reimagined for stereo, the music acquires an unusually enclosed character. Sounds seem unable to disperse, and repeated gestures linger, each return carrying greater psychological weight. Even the faint vocal traces remain caught within the surrounding texture, surfacing only briefly before dissolving back into the dense harmonic field. The closing “take the hindmost” provides the only substantial shift in perspective. Layers of electronic residue and circuitry redirect attention towards texture itself, as if searching for a new vocabulary from within the material already at hand. Nothing resolves. Instead, the album erases its own traces, leaving behind only the memory of sounds unwilling to disappear. The allow us to delve deeper into her personal heaven, Simi Fyda has kindly agreed to answer four questions by email. The album emerged from what you describe as “a version that almost existed” — music composed during a period of isolation and then reshaped into its final form. Could you talk about what was lost, what was retained, and whether you think traces of that unrealised version still haunt the record we hear today? I started the octophonic pieces during a period where I genuinely couldn’t make anything. I had no access to whatever I normally rely on. So I thought okay, let’s see if I still can do this. It was less of a decision and more just something to do, or to maintain. When I came back to it I was still kinda fed up with the whole thing, which actually helped. I stopped being careful with it and a lot got cut. But the atmosphere stayed, which annoyed me at first because I half wanted a clean break from it. I think that the earlier version is still in there somewhere, not as a foundation, probably more like the thing the record keeps almost touching without quite getting there. You have said that composing this music felt like becoming a demon — specifically one of the figures your grandmother claimed to have encountered in the very space where the album was eventually completed. How did that family story enter the work, and what does the title In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn reveal about the relationship between ancestry, memory, and self-transformation in your practice? I moved back into my grandmother’s apartment last November for a couple months and basically just disappeared into it. I wasn’t planning to make a record about any of that. I thought I was making something from a place rather than about it. She had paranoid schizophrenia, periods of seeing figures, demons, specific presences in specific corners of that apartment. I grew up hearing all of it, kind of terrified and fascinated at the same time. I lived there alone as a teenager too. So by the time I came back last november, it was already carrying a lot, I just wasn’t thinking about it consciously. She died in March, right after the album was finished. The timing still felt… I don’t even have a word to use here to be honest. The album isn’t about her, at least that wasn’t the intention. But she’s in there. Much of the album feels remarkably restrained. Tracks seem to hover on the verge of unleashing a full sonic assault, yet repeatedly pull back into themselves. Even the buried vocal traces feel half-suppressed, as though emerging from behind a wall. Was this tension between eruption and containment a conscious compositional strategy, or did it arise naturally from the material? Mostly conscious. I over-anticipate everything. I’ll have already resolved something in my head before it’s even happened, which just kills it. So a lot of this was genuinely trying not to do that. Whenever something felt like it was building toward release I’d just hold it there a bit longer than felt comfortable. I kept reminding myself that circling around something can be enough, that I don’t always have to arrive, don’t have to control every outcome in the ways I’ve conditioned myself to. The record is built around recurrence rather than development, with sounds, intervals, pipe tones and microtonal clusters reappearing in altered forms throughout the album. Given your background in installation and spatial sound, how did the process of collapsing an octophonic work into stereo affect your thinking about repetition, space and listening? Did reducing the physical dimensions of the piece paradoxically make it feel more intimate, claustrophobic, or psychologically charged? The recurrence came from spending a long time with a very small pool of material. At some point development just stopped making sense as a framework. Returning somehow did. In the octophonic versions sound could leave, it had a room to dissolve into. In stereo it couldn’t, so everything that was previously escapable became structural. The noise, the density, all of it just stayed there and then I brought it all even closer and it changed what the material actually was. I think space didn’t disappear, it just stopped being outside the work.

items.body: Since first joining the n5MD roster in 2013, Zaragoza has consistently expanded the artistic possibilities of the Ocoeur project. Greener Grass, Clearer Water represents another significant step forward, demonstrating an artist increasingly comfortable allowing restraint, patience, and subtlety to become primary compositional tools. One of Ocoeur’s most thoughtful and engaging works to date Greener Grass, Clearer Water by Ocoeur   Ocoeur has steadily refined a distinct artistic voice over more than a decade of releases on the n5MD label, but Greener Grass, Clearer Water feels like a particularly meaningful milestone. Franck Zaragoza has long demonstrated an exceptional sensitivity to texture, atmosphere, and emotional pacing, yet his eleventh full-length reaches an impressive level of restraint that proves deeply rewarding. Zaragoza embraces spaciousness and patience, allowing every sustained tone and subtle harmonic shift to carry remarkable emotional weight. The result is one of his most thoughtful and engaging works to date. Following the ecological themes introduced on Breath, Greener Grass, Clearer Water expands that vision into a fully beatless landscape where every composition unfolds with quiet confidence. There is an understated elegance throughout the record that never feels static. Instead, Zaragoza continually reshapes the listening experience through carefully layered drones, delicate piano figures, luminous synthesizer washes, and nearly imperceptible changes in density. His background in both classical composition and cinematic scoring becomes immediately apparent, not through grand gestures but through his remarkable command of pacing and emotional nuance. The opening sequence establishes the album’s character beautifully. “Clouds Never Die” introduces a serene sonic environment built from slowly unfolding harmonic movement and restrained orchestral textures. Zaragoza allows themes to emerge naturally from the interaction between sustained tones and gentle timbral variations. “Tomorrow, The Birds Will Sing” continues this approach with remarkable poise, offering subtle shifts in color that evoke openness and possibility without becoming sentimental. What makes Greener Grass, Clearer Water so compelling is its confidence in simplicity. Zaragoza understands that meaningful expression often comes through what is omitted rather than what is added. Each composition feels carefully considered, with no unnecessary embellishment competing for attention. Silence becomes an active compositional element, giving individual sounds room to resonate fully before yielding to the next carefully placed gesture. Every composition unfolds with quiet confidence :: Tracks such as “Lumières” and “Le chemin du retour” highlight Zaragoza’s remarkable ability to balance warmth with restraint. Rich harmonic layers bloom gradually before dissolving into softer passages that maintain an almost tangible sense of openness. The production is immaculate throughout, revealing countless subtle details during repeated listens. Gentle reverberation, carefully sculpted frequencies, and seamless transitions create an immersive environment that rewards attentive listening without ever demanding it. The album’s environmental perspective is equally successful because it avoids overt statements. Rather than illustrating ecological concerns through dramatic contrasts or heavy-handed symbolism, Zaragoza communicates through atmosphere alone. These compositions present imagined spaces where natural processes unfold with quiet dignity, encouraging reflection without prescribing conclusions. The emotional impact emerges organically through the music itself, allowing listeners to engage with the underlying themes on their own terms. The centerpiece, “Remember the Sea,” beautifully demonstrates Zaragoza‘s mature compositional voice. Broad harmonic movements rise and recede like slow tides, while distant textural elements provide an ever-changing backdrop that remains understated throughout. The piece captures a remarkable sense of scale while maintaining intimacy, a balance that few artists working within contemporary ambient music consistently achieve. The second half continues to deepen the album’s emotional resonance. “What Are You Running After?” introduces subtle harmonic tension before resolving into passages of remarkable clarity, while “Silences” explores the expressive potential of negative space with extraordinary precision. Even during its quietest moments, the album remains fully engaging because Zaragoza continuously shapes the listener’s attention through microscopic adjustments in texture and dynamics. Silence becomes an active compositional element :: “Blue Sky and Golden Leaves,” “Let Go,” and the closing “Your Smile” complete the journey with remarkable grace. Rather than building toward a dramatic conclusion, Zaragoza allows the album to settle naturally into a state of quiet equilibrium. It feels entirely appropriate that the final moments arrive without spectacle, leaving behind an enduring sense of balance instead of resolution. Since first joining the n5MD roster in 2013, Zaragoza has consistently expanded the artistic possibilities of the Ocoeur project. Greener Grass, Clearer Water represents another significant step forward, demonstrating an artist increasingly comfortable allowing restraint, patience, and subtlety to become primary compositional tools. It also continues n5MD‘s long tradition of championing artists who explore the intersection of electronic composition, modern classical sensibilities, and immersive sound with exceptional care and craftsmanship. Repeated listens reveal new relationships between harmonies, textures, and spatial details that are easy to overlook initially. That lasting depth ultimately becomes the album’s greatest strength. Greener Grass, Clearer Water is not interested in immediate impact or dramatic statements. Instead, it invites careful attention, rewarding listeners with a richly detailed and emotionally resonant experience that continues to unfold long after the final notes disappear. It stands among Ocoeur‘s finest achievements and serves as another outstanding addition to n5MD‘s consistently exceptional catalog. Greener Grass, Clearer Water is available on n5MD. items.body: Cosmos in Collision‘s Unwound arrives two years after The Passage of Time and confirms the direction of an ever-evolving project, capable of building dense and cinematic atmospheres. The cover artwork is an original watercolor by Cosmos in Collision, visually translating the narrative arc of the record: three chromatic fields blending from indigo to black, crossed by a white thread that slowly thins until it disappears. A conceptual work deeply rooted in both the real and supernatural worlds Electronic instrumental sounds exploring the lines between sci-fi, ambient, electronica, post-rock and shoegaze, featuring layers of ethereal guitars, cinematic atmospheres, shimmering soundscapes and intricate rhythmic textures that are combined to create an evocative dreamlike flow of unnatural and entirely enchanting sound. Unwound is a conceptual work deeply rooted in both the real and supernatural worlds inspired by the myth of the Three Fates. Each has a different role in weaving the destiny of the collective constant listeners. They are shapeshifters and guardians of the pathways into the earth and of the “limit” frontiers where it is believed that the supernatural most freely manifests itself. The trio are generally conceived of as sisters and are often given the names Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, which are the names of the Moirai, the version of the Fates who appear in Greek mythology. This trio is also found in Vedic Ṛta, the Avestan Asha (Arta), and the Egyptian Maat, as well as throughout some of ancient Northern Europe. These divine figures are often artistically depicted as beautiful maidens with consideration to their serious responsibility, which is specifically the life of each mortal. The traditional role of the Three Fates is to ensure that every being, mortal and divine, lives out their destiny as it was assigned to them by the laws of the universe. Some would say that Lachesis sings of the things that were, Clotho the things that are, and Atropos the things that are to be. Clotho with thread, Lachesis with an eye glass, and Atropos with scissors. Throughout history, Time has been an important subject of study in religion, philosophy, and science, and perhaps most of all in Music. The universe is infinite, which is distinctly an obsession (and perhaps an exclusive illusion) of humans. Multiple notions exist, and defining time in a manner applicable to all fields without circularity has consistently eluded much of the traditional scholarship. Here, on the extended player Unwound, the Fates shape the temporal sonic destiny of each human, expressed in textile metaphors, hence spinning fibers into yarn, or weaving threads on a loom. Time (again) is a fundamental part of this musical universe, perceived by events happening in a sequence, in a dimension, the moment the thread starts to wind into a form for the warp and woof of existence. The first track, “Breath (Clotho)” (5:30) opens like a sunrise, with a melodic and ethereal theme, evoking the first breath, easing in as a melody starts, forming a circular repeating, and richer fuller thicker experience as we go deeper into outer space, wary of shadowy, background figures who only really ever reveal their fateful secrets to people at the moment that their fates actually come to pass. Clotho is often depicted as a younger woman because of her relationship with the birth of humans. Three chromatic fields :: Track 2, “Unwound (Lachesis)” (7:33), is the measured beating heart of the EP, a long journey through the highs and lows of existence, carried by rhythmic textures and ever-shifting soundscapes. For mortals, this destiny has spanned their entire lives and is represented as that thread spun from a spindle. Once the circles start spinning, slowly at first, we are in touch with deep space and though there is no dominating beat, there is a tempo in the cycles here. These are each different dancing snowflakes, which are so soon melted into the aggregate exquisite liquid details. These overlapping elements combine and conflict in different ways. Lachesis (the allotter) calibrates the life under judgement, measuring out and determining the length of human life as if it were a thread, in the natural order which regulates and coordinates the operation of the universe. The combined measurements mark a specific moment in time from a reference point, or epoch. Perhaps the only important parts of the natural order are birth and death, remembering that time is neither an event nor a thing, and thus is not itself measurable nor can it be travelled, except, of course, on occasion in dreams. Atropos is traditionally pictured as an old woman because of her hand in the death of mortals. “Severance (Atropos)” (4:19) closes the release with a painful crescendo culminating in the final cut, inevitable and silencing. Atropos chooses the manner of each person’s death, and when their time has come, she cuts their life-thread with her famously abhorred shears. The rotating and revolving melodic weave suggests pondering fatalism, or the subjugation of all events or actions to a universal destiny, and the acceptance of the inevitability of the natural order of things. As the universe expands, some humans say that it pulls time with it because space and time are somehow linked as one. Cosmos in Collision‘s Unwound arrives two years after The Passage of Time and confirms the direction of an ever-evolving project, capable of building dense and cinematic atmospheres. The cover artwork is an original watercolor by Cosmos in Collision, visually translating the narrative arc of the record: three chromatic fields blending from indigo to black, crossed by a white thread that slowly thins until it disappears. Cosmos in Collision is a musical journey of Riccardo Spaggiari, who is based in Italy. Unwound is available on Sun Sea Sky. items.body: Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Force and sweetness intertwined Operational Ambivalence by Somatic Responses   Brothers John and Paul Healy have been operating as Somatic Responses out of Ammanford, a small industrial mining community in southwest Wales, since 1994. They formed in the hardcore acid techno scene, releasing their first material in 1995 before gradually expanding into industrial, drum and bass, noise, ambient, and breakcore territory. Their 1999 debut Circumflex on Hymen Records was a pivotal moment—taking their sound into new levels of complexity and intensity, and subsequent releases on Ad Noiseam, Sublight, Component, and their own Photon Emissions label built one of the most expansive and underappreciated catalogs in hard-edged electronic music. Key influence on rhythmic noise, breakcore, and IDM, yet somehow always operating just below the mainstream radar. The duo describe their work as “complex dislocated and broken beats, distorted intelligent constructions, fascinating sonic structures, force and sweetness intertwined.” Operational Ambivalence, it’s worth noting, credits “Everything by J.S.Healy“—making this a solo John Healy production, recorded in the Macro Chamber in Ammanford, rather than a full duo effort. The distinction is subtle but real. What you get with Operational Ambivalence is largely what you’d expect from the Somatic Responses catalog: distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout. It’s a 14-track self-released collection that feels like a gathering of material that belongs together rather than a concept album with a rigid arc. Tracks 8, 9, and 14 are the more ambient pieces of the release and still create beautiful visual imagery through technique. Out of that ambient batch, “H doesn’t fall down the stairs…” is the most interesting—not strictly ambient like the other two, but considerably softer in production than everything surrounding it. The lightness and strange composition here is compelling in its subtlety, drum rhythm play with light percussion and glitched patterns that sit between experimental and delicate. Distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout :: “New Shift” is another standout, with its intro of rolling clicks and sounds moving left to right across the stereo field, slowly manipulated kick drums coming in gradually as the track builds rhythm. What you thought was a softer track reveals itself as something larger entirely. The technique of building anticipation through percussion here is notable, it recalls the way Lexaunculpt constructed his pattern builds of glitches and various percussions on The Blurring of Trees (Planet Mu, 2003), that same slow accumulation of rhythmic detail until the structure reveals itself. The patterns here are interesting and the execution is patient. “Gatch” is another standout in all of its distortion and drumming. What makes it work compositionally is how it messes with pattern recognition, introducing drum patterns that redirect where you expect the track to go. The distortion is toned down carefully, which is harder than it sounds. Somatic Responses have always been comfortable in distortion’s territory, and John Healy demonstrates that comfort here, using strong distortion without making ears bleed, keeping it controlled enough that it serves the composition rather than overwhelming it. Using strong distortion without making ears bleed :: “Vital Ex Parts 1 and 2” earns its nine-minute runtime—two parts that feel like one extended piece assembled well. The drums in the introduction are playful before they introduce harsher builds, eventually transforming into something darker with ambient surroundings closing in. And “Residual Behaviour” is the track that’s hardest not to stop at simply because of how oddly it stands out in the context of everything else. Real drum samples playing in broken patterns with chords filling in the background—it sounds off, but there’s a strange beauty to it. The double hits, the stutters, the subtle chords and notes behind the rhythm, there’s no steady pulse here, just experimentation. When a rhythm starts forming it plays briefly before switching again, until the track ends on skips and rolls and hi-hats leading the outro with swishy drums. It sounds like it was a genuinely fun track to make, and that energy comes through in the listening. Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Artwork once again by Mattia Travaglini, whose visual language has become as much a part of the Somatic Responses aesthetic as the music itself. Operational Ambivalence is available on Bandcamp. Operational Ambivalence by Somatic ResponsesThe post Somatic Responses :: Operational Ambivalence (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. A producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next Kine 3 by Roel Funcken   The golden era of IDM left behind a particular kind of silence, not the absence of music, but the absence of the restless, process-driven curiosity that made that era feel alive. What’s left of it now echoes through the electronic music landscape in small signals, from old and new artists working in the margins. Roel Funcken has been one of those signals for over two decades, and Kine 3 is his loudest transmission yet—a massive tracklist, a substantial runtime, and the third installment of an ongoing series that began as a way of making sense of a large body of work. The Kine series, released through EC Underground—the South Florida-based multidisciplinary collective and label that has been bridging European and UK electronic music to US audiences since 2018, operates on a process-first logic: raw, modular, driven by hardware and intention rather than polish and structure. My first encounter with Roel‘s work came through a college radio station playing Funckarma‘s Part 3 EP on Djak-Up-Bitch, the Rotterdam-based Dutch label specializing in modern electronica and IDM distributed through Clone. That particular series was something, the melodic play and drum work had a freshness that aged remarkably well, still sounds lovely today. Fast forward years later and here we land with Kine 3. This album shows the maturity of Roel as a solo artist, distinct from the Funckarma project that first put him on the map alongside his brother Don. His productions here aren’t built around melodic composition in the conventional IDM sense, they’re explorative and experimental, each track following a particular pattern of letting effects and drums do the talking while atmospheric or melodic backgrounds grind immersively in the background. The loop continues :: With a tracklist this expansive, the best approach is to section it. Tracks 1 through 8 share similarities in style and composition — drums and effects leading, melodies surfacing immersively rather than announcing themselves. What Funcken does here shouldn’t be misread as pure improvisation. It’s closer to freeplay with intention, a distinction that matters. Modular synthesis and process-driven production naturally produce moments that feel unplanned, but behind every patch decision is a set of deliberate choices: which modules are connected, what triggers what, where the randomness is allowed and where it’s controlled. Funcken‘s approach on Kine 3 sits in that exact space—the results sound alive and unpredictable but the architecture holding them together is clearly considered. Track 9, “4ehmth,” functions as a divider. It’s the only track of the bunch that’s almost entirely drum play, and whether intentional or not, it creates a natural break between the first and second halves of the album. “Bydow 32” carries a distinct Funckarma feeling—a reminiscence of “Atomic” or “Finsbury Park” from Part 3, those same loose, melodic textures surfacing again through a different production context. “Dorphins” is another standout. Its melodic structure separates itself from the rest of the batch because the tweaking of the melody is being granularized at fast speeds, bouncing on a single note with harsh portamento bend stabs cutting through. Portamento—the gliding between pitches rather than jumping discretely, becomes a compositional tool here rather than just an effect. When applied fast and aggressively, it creates a pitch tension that sits between melody and noise, which is exactly what Funcken is exploiting. The drum structure across all these tracks is consistently loose and abrasive, not a loop so much as one long continuous rhythm that plays through rather than repeating. The two bonus digital tracks round things out distinctly. “Koidz” is heavier—distorted drums, more rhythmically aggressive than the core album, with a crunchy acid bass and what sounds like significant knob movement throughout. The emotional pads that come in give it a melodic tone that sticks to the structure as it plays, a ringing atmospheric pad leading the melody in a way the main album rarely does. “Kido” takes the same sound palette and reconfigures it—a different melodic composition built from similar material but toned differently, another take on the same logic but with its own feel of rhythm and structure. Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. He noted that sitting back and listening to Kine 1 with an audience changed something: the distance it created meant he was actually listening rather than judging. The support those releases received went straight back into the system—new Eurorack modules, extending the loop. Kine 3 is what that loop sounds like three iterations in, and it sounds exactly like what it is: a producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next, documenting the results with the confidence of someone who’s been doing this long enough to know when to get out of the way and let the process speak. EC Underground found the right home for it. The loop continues. Kine 3 is available on EC Underground. items.body: Birmingham MC Admiral Jerry, born Jerry Butler, cut “Up and Coming MC” and “Demonstrate” with UB40 in 1985. He is back with “Chant Down Babylon”, out on Windrush Day, 22 June, the date the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury in 1948. Butler grew up in Handsworth, a first-generation Black Briton of Jamaican heritage. Grammar school and a private education came next. The racism did not. “Growing up in Handsworth as a first-generation Black Briton, I experienced plenty of racist attitudes at grammar school and throughout my education,” he says. “This song is for oppressed people everywhere who are hoping and striving for a better tomorrow.“ The lyrics name Kunta Kinte, George Floyd and the Windrush Generation. Jerry works the riddim as a toaster, chatting across a roots reggae backing in the old sound system manner. Aldo Dice produced the track at his Farda Dice Studios in Birmingham for The Empire Windrush EP, with Sovereign Tugz and See No Equal on the mix and master. Jah Mission, the Amsterdam production house, shot the video across Birmingham and London. It settles on the Benjamin Zephaniah mural in Handsworth Park, unveiled in honour of the poet and activist on Windrush Day in 2024, the year after his death. More music from Jerry arrives in early 2027. Stream “Chant Down Babylon” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Admiral Jerry – Chant Down Babylon appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — David has moved from Biblical themes (Earth Rot and his interpretation of Handel's Messiah) to a forceful Broadway-like production about the plight of the African-American slave. David has also moved from Capitol Records to MCA.1. "Oh! Freedom" (1:20) David's personal rendering (with the help of Billie Barnum's chorus) of a traditional Black spiritual of the most powerful kind. The arrangement is totally a cappella with feeling as much of being outdoors (like an in-the-fields spiritual) as it is that of a church performance by a Baptist Gospel choir. Wow! (Apparently this version of the song was the one used in the soundtrack of the television mini-series of Arthur Haley's Roots.) (4.75/5)2. "The Auction" (6:43) after opening with a bluesy BB King-like guitar intro, the band enters and settles into a very funky motif over which the guitarist continues for a bit before the voice of Fleming Smith enters with the support of "ah-oo" vocals from a full choir in his background, Fleming narrating the somber and horrific event of a slave auction. The guitars, bass, horn section, and lead saxophone continue on high funk trajectory as a singular female singer and full choir present lines about the scene between Fleming's narrative sections. The lead sax, lead guitar, and wah-wah and rhythm guitars are awesome in here as James Hughart's bass just slays it throughout. My only complaint would be not being able to always clearly distinguish the words being sung by the choir. (9.5/10)3. "Sympathy" (5:43) vocal soloist Jessica Smith (The Ikettes, The Mirettes) sings an emotionally-powerful plaintive vocal over some beautiful ballad-like supporting smooth jazz. These are great blues performances with a lovely capture of the feel (and acoustics) of a back-woods shack in the swampy South. Great support from the band and orchestra--especially from James Hughart's double bass, Ernie Watts' flute, and Joe Sample's electric piano. I love the use of Maya Angelou's "I know why the caged bird sings" reference in the lyrics. With a performance like this it is surprising to me that the world has not really ever heard of Ms. Jessica Smith. (9.25/10)4. "Freedom" (4:29) a female choir dirges over funky-bluesy electric piano-led music. The guitar solo in the second and third minutes is jazz-bluesy in a kind of BB King way. A male choir enters in the third minute to put in their two cents worth before a saxophone solo takes over (Ernie Watts?). Joe Sample is quite active and good throughout this though mostly beneath the action on top. A turn-taking male-female, solo and choir conversational "dialogue" supercedes the music in the final minute. A song that oozes passion and suffering. (9.25/10)5. "The Leading Citizen" (5:08) a very funky mostly-instrumental jam which is peppered with choral discourse (between the male and female choirs) before coming into instrumental sections presenting guitar and sax solos over the constant, insistent, hard-driving music. Though an excellent funk groove with great musicianship and pace, there is something lacking in the variety/variation department and melody. (Perhaps it has to do with the monotony of the hard-driving music and male-only choir singing about the white master.) Some amazing bass, drums, percussion, and wah-wah electric guitar (probably by Motown god, David T. Walker). (9/10)6. "The Debt" (4:19) a piano jazz combo sounds like it's playing inside an old Southern back-woods juke joint as a Alexander St. Charles (pseudonym for Benard Ighner) sings in a Joe Williams-like baritone. What a cool, time-capturing performance and piece! (9/10)7. "Be Proud-My Race" (4:43) this piano and horns-dominated jazz-funk piece sounds more like an Off-Broadway moral-religious piece (like Godspell or Jesus Christ Superstar) as the full choir (and I mean full) belts out the full and constant lyrics--which are, apparently, a full-text rendering of the lyrics as adapted from Paul Laurence Dunbar's poem "Ode to Ethiopia," which were first published in 1905. Every time I've listened to this I find myself weeping uncontrollably by the second verse. The one personal criticism/adaptation that I make are with regards to the electric guitar and sax flourishes made between verses: they feel totally superfluous and unnecessary, even discourteous, and 2) the fact that the song only covers the first five of the poem's ten verses."Ode to Ethiopia / Compensation"O Mother Race! to thee I bring This pledge of faith unwavering, This tribute to thy glory. I know the pangs which thou didst feel, When Slavery crushed thee with its heel, With thy dear blood all gory. Sad days were those ? ah, sad indeed! But through the land the fruitful seed of better times was growing. The plant of freedom upward sprung, And spred its leaves so fresh and young? Its blossoms now are blowing. On every hand in this fair land, Proud Ethiope's swarthy children stand Beside their fairer neighbour; The forests flee before their stroke, Their hammers ring their forges smoke, They sit in honest labour. They tread the fields where honour calls; Their voices sound through senate halls In majesty and power. To right they cling; the hymns they sing Up to the skies in beauty ring, And bolder grow each hour. Be proud, my race, in mind and soul; Thy name is writ on Glory's scroll In characters of fire. High 'mid the clouds of Fame's bright sky Thy banner's blazoned folds now fly, And truth shall lift them higher. Thou hast the right to noble pride, Whose spotless robes were purified By blood's severe baptism. Upon thy brow the cross was laid, And labour's painful sweat-beads made A consecrating chrism. No other race, or white or black, When bound as thou wert, to the rack, So seldom stooped to grieving; No other race, when free again, Forgot the past and proved them men So noble in forgiving. Go on and up! Our souls and eyes Shall follow thy continuous rise; Our ears shall list thy story From bards who from thy root shall spring, and proudly tune their lyres to sing Of Ethiopia's glory.Because I had loved so deeply, Because I had loved so long, God in His great compassion Gave me the gift of song. Because I have loved so vainly, And sung with such faltering [breath],The Master in infinite mercyOffers the boon of Death.Text Authorship: by Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872 - 1906), "Ode to Ethiopia"I do not know why David Axelrod always bulldozed his way into public controversy (the death of his mother at age eight, the many traumatic events he encountered on the streets of lower-class Los Angeles, his youthful career as a successful boxer, his own struggles with addiction) but I so admire his fearless willful expression of empathy and public attention for the causes of the disenfranchised, downtrodden, and marginalized. (9.5/10) 8. "Oh! Freedom" (0:34)Total time: 32:59A-/five stars; marked down for brevity this is still a very powerful piece of music--one that begs for recognition for its historical significance as well as for its fine composition, rendering, and performances.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — STATICA by Avenged Sevenfold is an interesting experiment that possibly may be a teaser for a new album or some sort of overall conceptual piece. Having dealt with scientific and philosophical themes on their last 2 albums, this seems to be a critique on AI music, especially with the overall presentation of the lyrics. While musically this is very different from what they normally present, there is some nice guitar playing. The autotune is annoying, but it is overall part of the supposed concept. But this isn't what I look for in this band, but I guess I commend their daring and enthusiasm. I'd give this a low to mid 6 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is ASHES.

items.body: Review by Matti — - The First Review -Following Memoria that was released in early 2026, this fourth album of the Finnish Psych/Space Rock group HADAL SHERPA is the second posthumous work, ie. recorded between 2021-2025 under the leadership of multi-instrumentalist and composer Vesa Pasanen (1982 - July 2025). In my review for Memoria I said it to be their best album, but this time around I cannot feel equally positive. Except for Vesa's cover art which is much better than on the two preceding albums. Musically, however, the band doesn't much show progress or fresh ideas. They firmly operate within the familiar formula of riff-based instrumental space rock with some Eastern nuances, thus falling into the subgenre's major trap of sounding the same as before.The 38-minute album has seven tracks. 'Camel on Moon' (no use exoecting allusions to the certain British prog classic) has a rich soundscape even if the composition is pretty predictable. Indeed Hadal Sherpa's strength definitely isn't versatility in song structures but in the fine details of arrangements, but that justifies things only to a certain degree, and the band doesn't bring anything new to the table in that sense either. The next three rather fast pieces feel all the same as they are built on powerful riffs and do not contain notable variety in the tempo.Within the very first slow seconds of 'Return to Farum Azul' I felt happily relieved: finally a track completely different from the others! This dreamy, atmosperic piece may not be progressive enough to be the finest compositions in the band's catalogue, but it easily is the highlight of this album. Pi Viana's wordless chant is a nice addition. 'Mountains' has some beautiful flute from Pi, and there's something charming in its relatively laid-back atmosphere. I came to think of spaghetti westerns even if the music doesn't resemble Morricone's.The seventh track 'Gurbet' is composed by �zdemir Erdogan of whom I know nothing. Hadal Sherpa has done good work covering this undoubtedly Turkish tune. Piirpauke comes to my mind for the groovy spirit. All in all the happy surprise are quite scarce on this album. Perhaps it had already come to the point of scraping the bottom of the barrel, to construct another full album from the posthumous recordings? In any case, this release was (at least for me) totally unexpected. The band has said they won't be making new music without their deceased primus motor. For fans and friends, naturally it was a happy surprise nevertheless.

items.body: Review by blessed_of — Compassionizer tribute to Depeche Mode is a sincere and beautifully crafted homage that captures the emotional depth and melodic power of the original songs, while reimagining them through the band's unique avant-prog and ambient sensibility. Instead of simply reproducing familiar material, Compassionizer opens new dimensions?experimenting with texture, rhythm, and atmosphere to make each piece feel newly discovered. "But Not Tonight" opens the album with a warm, dreamy atmosphere. Where Depeche Mode's version glows with youthful melancholy, Compassionizer transforms it into a reflective meditation. "World Full of Nothing" and "The Things You Said" follow with chamber-like arrangements and subtle electronics, preserving the emotional fragility of the originals while reframing them through the band's layered and expressive sound. "Blue Dress" maintains the sensual minimalism of Depeche Mode but becomes more introspective and ethereal, while "Sibeling" expands into a sweeping ambient dialogue between piano, clarinet, and electronic textures. The closing "Enjoy the Silence" stands not as a cover but as a reimagining?slower, sacred, and contemplative. Where Depeche Mode's originals thrive on sleek synth- pop precision, Compassionizer adds warmth, introspection, and organic depth, creating not imitation but an honest conversation across time and genres. A beautiful, thoughtful, and deeply moving album.

items.body: Review by blessed_of — This seven-track masterpiece has become a personal favorite, with its rich musical depth and immersive atmosphere. Two tracks, in particular, have made a lasting impression: "I Feel Shine of the Day" and "For the Invisible Things." These compositions stand out not only for their intricate arrangements but also for their ability to evoke powerful emotions and introspective moments. The album, as a whole, feels like an intricate journey, crafted with immense care and dedication. It's clear that Compassionizer has invested a great deal of effort, resources, and time into creating this project. From the very first note to the final soundscape, you can sense the precision and intentionality behind each element. The group's ability to weave together diverse sounds and moods is truly remarkable, giving each track its own unique character while maintaining a cohesive narrative throughout. One of the most striking aspects of "The Fellowship of the Mystery" is the band's ongoing evolution. With every album, Compassionizer continues to refine and expand their sound, pushing boundaries and experimenting with new ideas. Their growth as artists is evident in this latest release, which feels like a natural progression from their previous work while also introducing fresh and innovative elements. The compositions are more layered, the instrumentation more dynamic, and the emotional resonance even deeper than before. What I particularly love about this album is its ability to transport the listener into different emotional states. "I Feel Shine of the Day" is a radiant, uplifting track that seems to encapsulate the essence of hope and light, while "For the Invisible Things" taps into more subtle, introspective emotions. The contrast between these two pieces, and the way the album shifts between moods, keeps the listener engaged and constantly discovering new layers of meaning. The production quality of the album is another highlight. Every sound feels meticulously placed, creating a soundscape that is both immersive and expansive. The textures and tones are rich, creating a listening experience that feels almost cinematic in scope. There's a sense of space and atmosphere that envelops the listener, making the music feel alive and breathing. In conclusion, "The Fellowship of the Mystery" is a testament to Compassionizer's artistry and their ability to create music that resonates on multiple levels. It's an album that rewards repeated listens, with each playthrough revealing new details and emotions. The band's commitment to their craft is palpable, and it's exciting to see where they will go from here as they continue to evolve and refine their sound. This is a must-listen for anyone who appreciates deep, thoughtful, and emotionally charged music.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Mental Architects are a very interesting math rock band from Bulgaria, that is unfortunately nolonger active. The trio consisting of Tony Velev (guitars), Nikki Ranguelov (bass), and MaxStoimenov (drums) tackles a rhythmically complex style that is simultaneously melodic, light-hearted, and digestible. Unlike many contemporary names in the math rock scene, MA have the peculiartendency to write fun and catchy sophisticated music, as you will often hear neat riffs and grooved-out chords on their 2012 studio album 'Celebrations', which is officially their third outing. Thereis an ostensible yet subtle post-rock aftertaste all over this record, but definitely not in theform of otherworldly crescendos or extended solos. The album is pretty playful and energetic, and tomy ears, one of the few math rock collections that could make you want to... dance?Why not; after all this is a celebratory album that impresses with a vast and flourishing guitarsound, often enough relying on multiple lines working around each other (this is a strong studioproject, above all), while the bass guitar and the drums, as tasty as they are, remain lessprominent, or even a little restrained, if you will. Had the band been more fusion-oriented, therhythm section could have been more unconventional and more prone to experimentation, but MentalArchitects' music is incredibly enjoyable, nonetheless. The compositions that certainly impress meon this album are 'Spell Shelter', 'Here Is Where, Where Better' (respectively the first and secondtracks), the 7-minute-long 'Caves of Keys', which is mesmerizing, and the song called 'Meth-Rock',which appears towards the end of the album. There is a joyous warmth to the music on 'Celebrations',which will appeal to many listeners, but that album cover... it's just alright.
